content: Identified a visual design flaw in Western music notation and proposed an alternative system to improve learnability for new musicians.
Designed a user experiment to test whether the redesign improved comprehension, and measured results across users with varying levels of musical experience.
Research was published at NCUR 2014, National Conference of Undergraduate Research. This was my first data visualization and UX research project.
Western music notation is largely intuitive: time reads left to right, pitch reads up and down.
However, vertical spacing is inconsistent. The same amount of vertical space can represent either a whole step or a half step depending on context.
Equal vertical space is given to major scale steps regardless of interval size, creating a visual encoding that misrepresents the underlying data.

alt: Figure showing how equal vertical spacing in traditional notation misrepresents whole steps and half steps
Figure showing the Circle Notation alternative where vertical spacing accurately reflects interval size

content: Hypothesis: this inconsistency creates a barrier to learning. The notation demands prior familiarity with the major scale structure rather than communicating it visually.
Designed an alternative system, Circle Notation (CN), where visual spacing accurately reflects interval size, addressing the identified design flaw directly.
Conducted a controlled experiment with participants across known levels of musical background: novice, intermediate, and expert.
Test consisted of paired visual and audio questions comparing Traditional Notation (TN) to Circle Notation (CN).
Results were statistically significant for novice and intermediate users. The redesigned notation outperformed the traditional system for learners who hadn't yet internalized scale structure.

alt: Side-by-side comparison of Traditional Notation and Circle Notation systems
Experiment results chart showing Circle Notation outperformed Traditional Notation for novice and intermediate users

content: Educational technology: adaptive music learning apps could use spatially accurate notation to lower the barrier for beginners. The research showed the strongest gains for novice and intermediate users, making this the most promising application.

Digital-native music tools: notation software like MuseScore or Sibelius is largely constrained by conventions designed for print. A digital context removes those constraints and opens the door to rethinking the visual encoding from the ground up.
Accessibility: a more consistent visual system may benefit learners with certain cognitive or learning differences who find the spatial inconsistencies of traditional notation a barrier to entry.

A meaningful design tradeoff to consider: Circle Notation did not outperform traditional notation for expert users, which makes sense. Experts have already internalized scale structure, so the inconsistency no longer registers as a problem. Any real-world implementation would need to consider how a learner transitions between systems as they advance, since optimizing for learnability and optimizing for mastery may require different design approaches.
